title: Recent directional selection measured in West Eurasian ancient DNA is near zero per SNP in ENCODE regulatory elements without mammalian conservation, below about a quarter of that in conserved ones
abstract:
Human regulatory DNA that mammals do not conserve carries almost none of the natural selection that changed allele frequencies in West Eurasia during the last 10,000 years, while conserved DNA carries much of it. This matters because one remaining argument for the function of such DNA is that it changes quickly by adaptation, and tests of purifying selection cannot see adaptation.

We used selection statistics for 9.7 million variants from an ancient-DNA time series of 15,836 people (Akbari et al. 2026). We applied stratified LD score regression (S-LDSC), which divides a genome-wide signal among classes of SNPs and corrects for linkage disequilibrium (LD, the correlation between nearby SNPs), to 1.1 million common SNPs. As a second method we fine-mapped selection loci. The classes were ENCODE candidate regulatory elements (cCREs) grouped by bases conserved across 241 mammals: tier 0 (no conserved base; 5.7% of SNPs) and tier 2 (5% or more conserved bases). The main measure is the conserved-equivalent fraction (CEF): the excess signal per SNP in tier 0 divided by the excess in tier 2 (0 = no excess; 1 = as much as conserved cCREs). We applied the same S-LDSC model to 106 independent genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of traits.

The tier-0 CEF was -0.06 in the main S-LDSC model (95% interval -0.39 to 0.24) and -0.08 to +0.11 in six models; in 5,324 fine-mapped loci it was -0.04 (-0.10 to 0.02). Per SNP, tier-2 cCREs had 12 times the genome-average selection signal (SE 2.5) and tier-0 cCREs 0.35 (SE 1.56). Trait heritability had the same pattern, so we found no sign that recent adaptation uses non-conserved cCREs more than trait variation does. Selection was more concentrated than heritability in functional DNA: coding SNPs (1.4% of SNPs) carried 34% of the selection signal, and coding enrichment (24, SE 4.7) and missense enrichment (67, SE 16) exceeded those of all 106 traits. Results were the same without SNPs near the strongest signals, without SNPs with possible batch effects, and for directly genotyped and imputed SNPs separately.

Limits: common SNPs and European LD only; absolute tier-0 values depend on the model, so the conclusion rests on CEF; the selection statistic can contain drift, structure and imputation effects; no independent ancient-DNA replication yet. An independent review found a weighting problem, which we fixed; the tier-0 result did not change.
